summary: Specifies version 7 of the Bundle Protocol for delay-tolerant networking, adapted from the experimental protocol in RFC 5050. It is designed for networks where connections can be long delayed or intermittent, such as in space. Data travels as bundles that are stored and forwarded when links become available. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Bundle Protocol version 7 (BPv7) moves data through delay-tolerant networks, where connections may be intermittent. Each node can store a bundle and forward it later, so the sender and receiver need not be connected at the same time.

how does bpv7 differ from rfc 5050
subtitle: A store-carry-forward protocol for networks with intermittent links and long delays.

tldr.problem: Ordinary network protocols assume a connected path, but delay-tolerant networks may have intermittent links, long or variable delays, and high bit error rates.
tldr.mechanism: Bundle Protocol version 7 packages data and metadata into CBOR-encoded bundles. Nodes store bundles and forward them when a suitable connection becomes available.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9171 standardizes BPv7, which is not interoperable with RFC 5050. RFC 9171 was later updated by RFC 9713 and RFC 9758.

today: RFC 9171 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 9713 and RFC 9758. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Delay-Tolerant Networks Use Bundles
sections.content:
Delay-Tolerant Networking addresses environments with intermittent connectivity, large or variable delays, and high bit error rates. Bundle Protocol version 7 (BPv7) operates above networks that may use different transport and network protocols.

BPv7 uses a store-carry-forward model: a node can retain data until it can forward it. The RFC does not define route computation, management of nodes, or how to secure bundles while they travel. BPv7 implementations do not interoperate with RFC 5050 implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks lose their connections for long periods or have very long delays. BPv7 lets data wait at a node until another connection becomes available.

sections.title: Nodes, Endpoints, and Services
sections.content:
A bundle node has a Bundle Protocol Agent, one or more optional convergence-layer adapters, and an application agent. The Bundle Protocol Agent runs the protocol; adapters send and receive bundles over underlying networks; the application agent supplies or receives application data.

A bundle is addressed to an endpoint, which is a set of zero or more nodes sharing an endpoint identifier. A node's administrative endpoint identifies the node. The protocol itself does not guarantee end-to-end delivery; applications or extensions must provide that assurance when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node has protocol software, adapters for its connected networks, and an application that supplies or receives data. An endpoint identifier can name one node or a group of nodes.

sections.title: The Bundle Structure
sections.content:
A bundle is a CBOR indefinite-length array containing at least two blocks. It begins with exactly one immutable primary block, followed by one or more canonical blocks, and ends with exactly one payload block and a CBOR break code.

The primary block carries destination and source endpoint identifiers, a report-to endpoint, creation timestamp, lifetime, and flags. Canonical blocks carry their type, number, processing flags, optional CRC, and type-specific data. CRC type 0 means none, type 1 means X-25 CRC-16, and type 2 means CRC32C.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle is a structured container with addressing and timing information, optional extra blocks, and one payload block. The payload block carries the application data.

sections.title: Receiving, Forwarding, and Expiring Bundles
sections.content:
When a node receives a bundle, it checks its structure and any attached CRCs. It then delivers the payload if the node belongs to the destination endpoint, or selects a next node and convergence-layer adapter for forwarding.

A bundle remains stored while it has retention constraints. It expires when its age exceeds its lifetime and the node must delete it. A node may fragment a bundle to fit a contact, and a destination can reassemble fragments with the same source node ID and creation timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: A node checks a received bundle, then delivers it locally or keeps it for forwarding. It deletes an expired bundle, and fragments can be joined again at the destination.

sections.title: Extension Blocks and Status Reports
sections.content:
BPv7 defines Previous Node, Bundle Age, and Hop Count extension blocks. The hop limit must be from 1 through 255; a node should delete a bundle whose hop count exceeds that limit.

A source can request status reports about reception, forwarding, delivery, or deletion. Because one bundle can generate many reports along a path, status-report generation MUST be disabled by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra blocks can record which node forwarded a bundle, its age, or its hop count. Status reports can describe bundle progress, but they are off by default to avoid excessive traffic.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec) provides bundle security services through separate blocks. The RFC requires a Bundle Protocol Agent that sources, verifies, or accepts bundles to implement BPSec support, though using it for a particular bundle is optional.

Convergence-layer protocols must provide rate limiting or congestion control because long round-trip times make reactive end-to-end congestion control unsuitable. RFC 9171 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 9713 and RFC 9758.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate security blocks can protect bundles while they wait or travel, and each underlying network connection must control its traffic rate. RFC 9713 and RFC 9758 later updated this Proposed Standard.
